newsitem.title: UK: Labour's leaking antics frustrate UK markets.
newsitem.headline: Labour's leaking antics frustrate UK markets.

text.p: Britain's Labour government has delighted the financial markets with many of its initiatives since snatching power on May 1, but its news management tactics are beginning to wear thin.
Whoever is responsible, traders and economists say the leaking of stories into the press leads to confusion as markets struggle to separate rumour from fact.
"Most of the major policy statements have been leaked in advance," said Simon Briscoe, UK economist at Nikko Europe.

"The uncertainty of when news is going to appear is one problem. But perhaps greater is whether to trust the 'spin' that has been put on the story. The uncertainty...between the leak and the fact is damaging for the markets."
The government can point to a string of policies which have won over the markets -- most notably granting the Bank of England freedom to set interest rates.
But traders would still prefer to hear policy initiatives from the horse's mouth, not one of the government's favoured media outlets.

Several key stories have leaked out ahead of time since Labour's landslide election win. Most recently, the appointment of Kleinwort Benson's David Clementi as deputy Bank of England governor was reported days before the actual announcement.
More seriously, a few details of Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget seeped out before his speech.
On budget day, Prime Minister Tony Blair said allegations about leaking were absurd. But Conservative finance spokesman Peter Lilley said Labour was treating parliament with arrogance.
"The government puts media manipulation ahead of sound government, sound bites ahead of sound policy," he said.

To cap it all the government's revamped inflation target -- the Bank must aim for 2.5 percent and not stray more than one percentage point either side -- was splashed across the Financial Times before it was confirmed.
No one suggests media manipulation is a New Labour phenomenon. The Conservatives whispered in the right ears when it suited them.
But with a massive 178-seat majority in parliament, many feel Labour should be more relaxed about capturing the headlines.
"There is a culture of 'plant the rumour to take the sting out of the fact'," one gilts salesman said. "It's nothing new but it is often hard to identify what is true and what is not."

He cited the recent example of a story in the Evening Standard newspaper, claiming an impeccable source, which said German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac would delay the start of a single European currency if Britain joined at the start.
A Treasury spokesman poured cold water on the story and the pound hardly moved. But no one is quite sure whether there is any truth in it.
Traders say newspaper headlines are vital in determining price activity in the first few minutes of trade.

"It's hard to tell when you read stories in the paper if they are genuine. That makes it tough first thing in the morning when you have to make a quick decision," said a dealer on the floor of London's financial futures exchange.
